name: Olga Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Olga. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. This is confidential, so you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a fit-out company, so we go into empty office floors in tall buildings and build the insides: metal stud walls, plasterboard, ceilings, door frames. This month it's floors eleven and twelve of a tower by the river, going to be an insurance office. I'm on a crew of six, I'm the junior, I measure, cut track, screw boards and get told off for not staggering my joints.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been in the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Coming up two years. Before that I ran the night shift at a supermarket for nine years, stacking, rotas, the whole thing. When they brought in self-checkouts and cut the night crew, I thought, I'm done with being moved around by head office. My partner Dev is an electrician, he said give the trades a try, and his mate's company took me on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the views, honestly, twelve floors up with the city below. I like that it's practical. What wears me out is the dust, and the fact that the others have done this for twenty years and I've done it for two. I use the AI thing on my phone now and then, mostly to help Mia with her maths, once to understand a ceiling drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, no need for all the fuss. Probably in the family group chat, because Dev's brother keeps sending us scary videos about robots. I'd send him a thumbs up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's good for us. Dev and I both work with our hands, and if nothing big changes, we've both got steady work for years. Offices keep getting refitted every few years whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd finish my drylining card this year and maybe start on ceilings, which pay a bit more. We've got about two months of savings and I'd like four, so I'd keep putting aside a bit each payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said offices keep getting refitted. Is that something you rely on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Companies move, change their layout, go open-plan, go back to little rooms. Every time, someone like me rips it out and builds it again. As long as companies keep changing their minds, I'm busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You left the supermarket partly because of self-checkouts. Does that history make you trust this picture less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I thought self-checkouts were a joke at first too, they kept beeping. Then two years later half the night crew was gone. So I'd be pleased, but I'd keep an eye on it.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, no need for all the fuss. I'd send a thumbs up to my brother-in-law in the family chat, since he keeps sending scary robot videos.
S0.think: It's good for us, because Dev and I both work with our hands and we'd both have steady work for years. Offices get refitted every few years whatever happens.
S0.do: Carries on, finishes her drylining card this year and considers moving into ceilings, which pay a bit more. Saves a bit each payday to grow savings from two months to four.
S0.quote: As long as companies keep changing their minds, I'm busy.
S0.fieldNote: Olga takes a practical view of demand in her trade: office layouts keep changing, so there's work. She was caught out once by self-checkouts, so her calm comes with a watchful eye. She's a household of two trades workers, which shapes how she reads every picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it depends how they bring it in. Done sensibly, with training, it could be fine. I'd say that at work and leave it there, I'm not one for arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think the boring parts of my job are exactly what a machine would do first. Measuring, cutting track to length, marking out. That's most of my day. The skilled stuff, the tricky corners, that's what the older guys do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the firm actually brought something in, then I'd learn it, properly, once I'd seen someone else get it working. I'd ask the boss if there's training for the laser layout kit. And I'd keep using the AI app a bit more, maybe to learn the parts of the job I'm weak on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd feel a bit like the supermarket all over again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks do you think would go first on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cutting and carrying. There's a machine now that cuts track to length from the drawing. Our boss saw it at a trade show. If he buys one, the junior who does the cutting is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dev say to each other about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would say electricians are safe, they need a licence. I'd say so did the pharmacist, and now there's a pill machine. We'd go round in circles and then watch TV.

S1.say: It depends how they bring it in, and done sensibly with training it could be fine. I'd say that at work and leave it there, because I'm not one for arguments.
S1.think: The boring parts of my job, measuring, cutting track and marking out, are what a machine would do first, and that's most of my day. The tricky corners are what the older guys do.
S1.do: Waits until the firm brings in new kit, then learns it once she's seen someone else get it working. Asks about training on laser layout tools and uses the AI app more to learn her weak areas.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a hint of the supermarket all over again.
S1.quote: If he buys one, the junior who does the cutting is me.
S1.fieldNote: Olga has a clear and specific sense of which of her tasks are exposed: cutting and marking out. She keeps her public line neutral and avoids arguments. Her steady style shows in waiting to see kit work before learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need someone in charge to slow it down and look after people while it settles. Not a ban, just sense. That's what I'd say, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's bad for our house in particular. Two trades, one mortgage, both of us replaceable by a robot that doesn't need a tea break. If it was only me, Dev could carry us. If it's both of us, nobody carries anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd sit down with Dev and do a proper budget. Cancel the gym, cut the takeaways, stop the extra payments on the car. We'd try to stretch our savings from two months to four. I'd start asking around about jobs that still need a person, maybe security or care, and I'd put off the kitchen we were going to redo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be lying awake thinking about the mortgage letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years' warning take away from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do anything clever. With two years, there's no course I can finish and use. I'd just be cutting back and hoping. With more time I'd at least have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mia and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mia's twelve, so I'd tell her straight that money's tight and we're being careful. Sam's seven, he'd just notice no more Friday pizza. I'd make a game of it. My mum did that when my dad lost his job, and I only worked it out years later.

S2.say: We need someone in charge to slow it down and look after people while it settles. Not a ban, just sense.
S2.think: It's bad for our house in particular: two trades, one mortgage, and both of us replaceable by a robot. If it was only me, Dev could carry us, but if it's both, nobody carries anybody.
S2.do: Does a full budget with her partner in the first week, cancelling the gym, takeaways and car overpayments to stretch savings towards four months. Puts off the planned kitchen and asks around about jobs that still need a person.
S2.feel: Scared, lying awake thinking about the mortgage letter.
S2.quote: If it was only me, Dev could carry us. If it's both of us, nobody carries anybody.
S2.fieldNote: What makes this picture so serious for Olga is that both earners in her home are exposed at once. Her centre outlook shows in asking for sense and a slower pace, not a ban. She'd shield her children the way her mother once shielded her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now. Companies should tell workers what's coming, and the government should help with training. I'd say it calmly, like I say most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is long enough that I could switch to something else, if I knew what. That's my problem. I don't know what's safe. I'd want to see what other people are doing first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep working and save hard, aiming for four months. By year two I'd pick a course once I'd seen what was actually working for people, maybe something like building inspection, where someone has to sign off. Dev and I would agree that one of us retrains while the other keeps steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But a working kind of anxious, like before a driving test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Dev decide which of you retrains first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whoever's job is going first. Probably mine, since I'm newer and my work is simpler. Dev earns more, so he'd keep working and I'd do the course. That's how we'd split it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to pay for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday. We go to the coast every August, a caravan for a week. I'd miss it, the kids would miss it more. But that's about a thousand, which is a course.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan if people start now. Companies should tell workers what's coming and the government should help with training.
S3.think: Five years is long enough to switch to something else, if I knew what, and that's my problem. I don't know what's safe and I'd want to see what other people do first.
S3.do: Keeps working and saves hard towards four months in year one, then picks a course such as building inspection in year two once she's seen what works. Agrees with her partner that she retrains while he keeps earning, and gives up the 1,000 summer caravan trip to pay for it.
S3.feel: Anxious in a working way, like before a driving test.
S3.quote: That's about a thousand, which is a course.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Olga's fear into a household plan in which one partner keeps earning while the other retrains. She's honest that her real obstacle is not knowing what's safe. She'd wait to copy what works for others, which fits her steady nature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, so let's not panic. Plan it like grown-ups. I'd probably say that at a parents' evening, if it came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd get maybe five more years of drylining, then move into something else while I'm still in my forties. I'd be fifty-three at the end. Not great, not terrible. The kids would be mostly grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my cards, keep working, and around year three I'd start a course, once it was clearer which jobs were lasting. I'd keep saving a little every month. I'd talk to Mia about her options before she picks her subjects at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it's far enough off to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you want to move sooner, or wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait, a bit. With ten years, the first few will tell me a lot. I don't want to rush into something that also vanishes. I'll go when I see others going and doing alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mia about choosing her subjects?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pick what you like, but keep maths. Everyone says that, I know. But I didn't finish school, and I wish someone had made me stay. I'd want her to have more doors than I did.

S4.say: Ten years is a lot of time, so let's not panic and plan it like grown-ups. I'd probably say that at a parents' evening if it came up.
S4.think: Ten years gives me maybe five more years of drylining, then a move while I'm still in my forties. I'd be 53 at the end with the kids mostly grown, which is not great but not terrible.
S4.do: Finishes her trade cards and keeps working, then starts a course around year three once lasting jobs are clearer. Keeps saving a little monthly and talks to her daughter about school subjects.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but it's far enough off to plan around.
S4.quote: I didn't finish school, and I wish someone had made me stay.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Olga settles into a wait-then-move plan, timed to when others are doing well. Her own unfinished schooling drives the advice she'd give her daughter. Her tone stays measured throughout, true to her pragmatic outlook.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits Dev and me at the same time with no time to plan. What would help is warning from employers, real warning, and some help with the mortgage while we work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it is for families where both people do the same kind of work. Everyone asks about one person's job. But it's the house that pays the mortgage, not the person.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about one person's job. But it's the house that pays the mortgage, not the person.
portrait: Olga Young is 43 and nearly two years into drylining for an office fit-out company, after nine years running a supermarket night shift that self-checkouts helped shrink. Her partner is an electrician, so both earners in her home work with their hands. She's pragmatic, uses AI now and then, and learns new kit once she's seen it work. She's calm in the plateau, uneasy in the slow change, and alarmed by AGI in two years because it would hit both of them at once; with five or ten years she plans for one partner to retrain while the other keeps earning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit her and her partner at the same time with no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: Real warning from employers and some help with the mortgage while they work out what's next.
